html:
The map's label for the Muslim trading towns of the East African coast, from Mogadishu in the north to Kilwa in the south, shown from 1000 to 1600. Most of them are better known as the Swahili city-states.

Each town was independent, ruled by its own sultan or council of merchant families, and built in coral stone around a mosque and a harbour. They lived from the monsoon trade of the Indian Ocean, sending gold, ivory, timber and enslaved people north and east, and buying cloth, beads and Chinese porcelain.

The leading towns:

  • Mogadishu, which grew rich in the 1200s and 1300s and minted its own coins;
  • Malindi and Mombasa, long rivals on the Kenyan coast;
  • Kilwa, which controlled the gold trade from Great Zimbabwe through the port of Sofala and built the Great Mosque and the palace of Husuni Kubwa.

The traveller Ibn Battuta visited Mogadishu, Mombasa and Kilwa in 1331 and praised Kilwa as one of the finest cities in the world. Chinese ships of Zheng He's fleet called at Malindi in the 1410s.

Everything changed when the Portuguese arrived in 1498. They sacked Kilwa and Mombasa in 1505, forced the towns to pay tribute, and built Fort Jesus at Mombasa in 1593. In the north, the inland Ajuran state and later Somali powers held the Benadir coast. Omani Arabs drove the Portuguese out of the coast north of Mozambique by 1698.
